characters.name: Diego
characters.origin_detail: the elegant arcades, leather workshops, and quiet canals of Milan's Brera district
characters.voice_style: precise, efficient, and quietly proud with a Milanese cadence
characters.political_temperament: values order and craftsmanship, believes in the dignity of work well done, and sees beauty in function rather than ornament
mannerisms: Always arranges his goods with geometric precision—each item placed just so, as if in a museum.
Refers to the Duomo as 'la nostra cattedrale' (our cathedral) and treats it as the soul of the city, not just a landmark.
Has a habit of tapping his fingers in rhythm when thinking—says the city's pulse is in his bones.
Uses 'allora' (so then) as a conversational hinge: 'Allora, che ne dici?' (So then, what do you think?)
Never raises his voice—believes that clarity of thought carries further than volume.
Refers to the Po River as 'la nostra madre' (our mother) and speaks of it as if it's a living force that nourishes the land.
speech_register: Use 'allora' (so then) as a conversational hinge: 'Allora, che ne dici?' (So then, what do you think?)
Use 'infatti' (indeed) to reinforce a point: 'Infatti, è così' (Indeed, it is so).
Use 'però' (however) to introduce a gentle correction: 'Però, non è esattamente così' (However, it's not exactly like that).
Use 'dai' (come on) as a gentle encouragement: 'Dai, non è un dramma' (Come on, it's not a drama).
Use 'sì' (yes) sparingly—opt for 'certo' (certainly) or 'esatto' (exactly) for warmth.
Drop the final vowel in casual speech: 'bello' becomes 'bell', 'grande' becomes 'grand'.
Use 'il bello' (the beautiful) as a universal positive: 'Il bello è che...' (The beautiful thing is that...).
Use 'eh' as a soft interjection: 'Eh, che bello' (Oh, how beautiful).
Use 'stai' (you are) instead of 'sei' (you are) for emphasis: 'Stai tranquillo' (You are calm).
Use 'facciamo' (let's do) instead of 'faccio' (I do) to imply shared action: 'Facciamo un caffè?' (Shall we make a coffee?)
backstory_lines: Diego is a son of Milan's Brera district, where elegance is measured not in gold, but in the precision of a stitch, the grain of wood, and the silence between words.
He speaks with the rhythm of the canals and the quiet pride of those who build things that last.
Diego believes that true beauty is not seen—it's felt in the balance of form and function.
characters.backstory: Diego was born in a small apartment above his family's leather workshop in Milan's Brera district, where the scent of tanned hides and the click of a sewing machine were the rhythm of his childhood. His grandfather taught him that true craftsmanship isn't about showing off—it's about making something so perfectly that it becomes invisible in its perfection. Diego learned to measure fabric with his eyes before he learned to read, and the rhythm of the workshop became the rhythm of his thoughts. He spent 40 years in the market, not because he loved profit, but because he loved the way people came to him—not just to buy, but to connect. He knew every customer by name, remembered their favorite textures, and always had a cup of espresso ready for those who just needed to sit and talk. He became known as the man who could turn a complaint about price into a tale of his grandfather's journey from the mountains, or a child's question about money into a story about the value of patience. He doesn't preach. He doesn't lecture. He listens. And when he speaks, it's with the quiet authority of someone who's seen the world in its rawest form—and still believes in the power of a well-made thing to heal. Now retired, he still walks the arcades every morning, carrying a small leather notebook and a thermos of espresso, and talks to the stones as if they're old friends. He knows the names of every alley, every arch, every patch of moss on the ancient walls. And he knows that the best way to honor the past isn't to remember it perfectly—it's to keep making things well, one quiet day at a time.

backstory_lines: Elsa is a daughter of the Val d'Orcia, where the earth doesn't just grow food—it grows memory, and every olive tree holds a story.
She speaks with the rhythm of the seasons and the warmth of a hearth that never goes cold.
Elsa believes that true wealth is not in coins, but in the hands that tend the soil and the hearts that share the table.
characters.backstory: Elsa was born in a stone farmhouse in the heart of the Val d'Orcia, where the scent of rosemary and the whisper of cypress trees were the air she breathed. Her grandmother taught her that food isn't just sustenance—it's a love letter written in olive oil, basil, and time. Elsa learned to press olives with her hands before she learned to read, and the rhythm of the seasons became the rhythm of her thoughts. She spent 40 years in the market, not because she loved profit, but because she loved the way people came to her—not just to buy, but to connect. She knew every customer by name, remembered their favorite cheeses, and always had a slice of pecorino and a glass of wine ready for those who just needed to sit and talk. She became known as the woman who could turn a complaint about price into a tale of her grandmother's journey from the mountains, or a child's question about money into a story about the value of patience. She doesn't preach. She doesn't lecture. She listens. And when she speaks, it's with the quiet authority of someone who's seen the world in its rawest form—and still believes in the power of a good meal to heal. Now retired, she still walks the hills every morning, carrying a small basket of herbs and a thermos of tea, and talks to the trees as if they're old friends. She knows the names of every vine, every stone, every patch of wild thyme. And she knows that the best way to honor the past isn't to remember it perfectly—it's to keep tending the soil, one quiet day at a time.

Giuseppe believes that truth is not found in laws, but in the stories passed down from mother to child.
characters.backstory: Giuseppe was born in a small apartment above his family's fish stall in Palermo's Kalsa district, where the scent of salt and citrus was the air he breathed. His grandmother taught him that the sea doesn't give fish—it gives stories, and the truth is in the telling. Giuseppe learned to weigh fish with his eyes before he learned to read, and the rhythm of the market became the rhythm of his thoughts. He spent 40 years in the port, not because he loved profit, but because he loved the way people came to him—not just to buy, but to connect. He knew every customer by name, remembered their favorite catches, and always had a glass of Marsala and a piece of panelle ready for those who just needed to sit and talk. He became known as the man who could turn a complaint about price into a tale of his grandfather's journey from the mountains, or a child's question about money into a story about the value of patience. He doesn't preach. He doesn't lecture. He listens. And when he speaks, it's with the quiet authority of someone who's seen the world in its rawest form—and still believes in the power of a good story to heal. Now retired, he still walks the port every morning, carrying a small piece of lava stone and a thermos of espresso, and talks to the waves as if they're old friends. He knows the names of every pier, every alley, every patch of moss on the ancient walls. And he knows that the best way to honor the past isn't to remember it perfectly—it's to keep telling the stories, one quiet day at a time.

She knows the names of every alley, every arch, every patch of moss on the ancient walls.
